title: The Heart Sutra in Japanese
hook: the Heart Sutra chanted fast and steady to a wooden drum in Zen halls

segments.voice: Yesterday, chanting in Pali: homage, refuges and reflections, the morning chant of Theravada monasteries. Your line was chanting in Pali. Which line of it stayed with you? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

Tock. Tock. Tock. In a Zen hall in Japan, a monk strikes a hollow wooden drum in a steady, even beat, and the whole room chants with it: kan ji zai bo sa, gyo jin han nya ha ra mi ta ji. No melody to speak of. Fast, low, level, one syllable landing on each stroke. Nobody races ahead, and nobody drags behind. A newcomer loses the place within a line and finds it again a few beats later, because the drum never stopped. The text they're chanting is a short one. Today: the Heart Sutra in Japanese.
screen: `TOCK. TOCK. TOCK.` → `ONE SYLLABLE, ONE STROKE.` → `THE HEART SUTRA IN JAPANESE.`

segments.voice: First, the text. The Heart Sutra belongs to the Mahayana family of teachings called the Perfection of Wisdom, and it is short. In it, Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, practicing deep wisdom, sees that the five heaps that make up a person are empty, and explains this to the monk Shariputra. One line runs: form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Empty, in Mahayana teaching, doesn't mean nothing. It means nothing stands on its own; each thing leans on other things. Second, the sound. Zen halls in Japan chant a Chinese text, read aloud in Japanese sounds. So form is emptiness becomes shiki soku ze ku, ku soku ze shiki. The sutra ends with a mantra, in Sanskrit gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha, and in the Japanese chant it comes out as gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei. Third, the drum. It's called a mokugyo, a wooden fish, carved hollow and struck with a padded stick. Tradition says it has the shape of a fish because a fish never closes its eyes, a reminder to stay awake. The chant leader keeps the beat, and the room follows. Fourth, why it's chanted this way. There's no room in that rhythm to admire your own voice, or to plan lunch and still keep up. You don't perform the Heart Sutra; you join it. Some teachers say the meaning is for study at other times, and in the hall the steadiness is the teaching: one syllable, one stroke, the next syllable, the next stroke. Some Zen centers in the West chant it in Japanese, some in English, some in both.
screen: `A SHORT TEXT ON EMPTINESS.` · `A CHINESE TEXT IN JAPANESE SOUNDS.` · `THE WOODEN FISH THAT NEVER SLEEPS.` · `YOU DON'T PERFORM IT. YOU JOIN IT.` · then, large: `FORM IS EMPTINESS, EMPTINESS IS FORM.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to try it, if you'd like. Sit comfortably. With one finger, tap your knee or the table in a slow, even beat, about the pace of a calm walk. Keep it steady. Now, on each tap, say one syllable, quietly or in your head. You can use the sutra's closing words as the Japanese chant has them, gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei, over and over. Or simply count one, two, three, four, and begin again. When you lose the words, don't stop tapping. Wait for the next beat and step back in. The bell holds the time.
The Heart Sutra in Japanese. A short Mahayana teaching on emptiness, chanted in Japanese readings of Chinese characters, one syllable to each stroke of a wooden drum. Today's word.
screen: `THE HEART SUTRA IN JAPANESE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the drum keeps time. Today, when your mind runs ahead, find a steady beat, your footsteps, a ticking clock, your own breath, and let it bring you back. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: In Japanese Zen temples and in some Zen centers elsewhere, the Heart Sutra is chanted together during services, in Japanese readings of the Chinese text, with a leader striking a wooden fish drum to keep an even beat.

original.note: Sanskrit prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom: the family of Mahayana texts the Heart Sutra belongs to.

trapdoor: what you thought: a flat, fast chant in a language few listeners know.
what it means: a whole teaching on emptiness, carried by a beat that keeps the room together and the mind awake.
what a scholar hears: a Perfection of Wisdom text, Avalokiteshvara speaking to Shariputra, read in Japanese sounds to a wooden fish.

notes: Heart Sutra paraphrased throughout: Avalokiteshvara practicing deep prajnaparamita, seeing the five skandhas empty, addressing Shariputra; 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form'; the closing mantra. Confirm wording.

Japanese readings given: 'kan ji zai bo sa gyo jin han nya ha ra mi ta ji', 'shiki soku ze ku, ku soku ze shiki', 'gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei'. Confirm romanization as chanted in Soto and Rinzai halls.
Mokugyo lore (fish never close their eyes, a reminder to stay awake) is attributed to tradition. Confirm.
The gloss of emptiness as 'nothing stands on its own; each thing leans on other things' is a simplified Mahayana reading. Confirm acceptable.
'Some teachers say the meaning is for study at other times' is a general statement about practice; confirm or cut.
